title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Data Center Coalition to the answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. and certain other comments and answers re the proposal to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service et al. under ER26-3515.

documents.name: DCC Answer - Final.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                         )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                              )                   Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                         )

                           MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER
                     AND ANSWER OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION

        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”),1 the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”)2

hereby moves for leave to answer3 and answers the answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(“PJM”)4 and certain other comments and answers filed by intervenors regarding PJM’s proposal

to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) and a Large Load Registry.5

I.      ANSWER

        As DCC explained in detail in its Protest, DCC strongly supports reforms to ensure that

large loads can be integrated into the grid while preserving reliability and protecting customers.




        1
           18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213.
        2
           DCC is a membership organization of leading data center owners and operators. Public testimony and
written comments submitted by DCC do not necessarily reflect the views of each individual DCC member. A list of
current DCC members is accessible at https://www.datacentercoalition.org/members.
         3
           DCC acknowledges that the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure do not typically allow answers
to answers. However, the Commission has accepted answers in the past when they have (i) assisted the Commission
in understanding the issues presented, (ii) provided additional information for the Commission’s decision-making
process, and (iii) helped ensure an accurate record. See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶ 61,162, at P
29 (2022); Canal Generating LLC, 181 FERC ¶ 61,157, at P 14 (2022); Equitrans, L.P., 134 FERC ¶ 61,250, at P 6
(2011); Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., 132 FERC ¶ 61,023, at P 16 (2010). In this proceeding, DCC’s answer will
help the Commission understand the issues presented by PJM and the other answers and comments filed in this
proceeding and provide further information related to the issues in this proceeding to inform the Commission’s
decision-making process. DCC therefore respectfully requests leave to file this answer and asks the Commission to
consider this answer in its deliberations in this proceeding.
         4
           PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (Sept. 23, 2026) (“PJM Answer”).
         5
           PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to
Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability (Aug. 13,
2026) (“Filing”).
 Along with the Virginia State Corporation Commission, DCC has called on states to develop

model interruptible tariffs and load-reduction programs that would allow large loads to take

interruptible service. DCC shares PJM’s commitment to ensuring that large load growth occurs in

a way that is compatible with reliability and does not result in cost shifts to other customers.

       But PJM’s proposal to impose a region-wide retail curtailment framework represents an

unprecedented intrusion into the authority reserved to the states under the Federal Power Act

(“FPA”) that must be rejected. Facing strong opposition in this proceeding from a range of parties

including state regulators, utilities, generation owners, and data center developers, PJM’s Answer

attempts to recast IRAS as focused exclusively on the wholesale markets. But the highly curated

set of statements that PJM cites in support of this interpretation cannot overcome the

overwhelming record evidence demonstrating that IRAS targets, and seeks to dictate, the rates,

terms, and conditions of retail service. PJM’s acknowledgment that IRAS requires enlisting

Electric Distributors and state regulators to implement PJM’s directives highlights that IRAS

treads into areas that are beyond PJM’s and FERC’s jurisdiction. IRAS would invert the regulatory

divide established by the FPA by imposing a federally approved retail curtailment framework

where state authorities are charged with conforming their retail curtailment and compensation

practices to align with PJM policy.

       PJM continues to claim that states will be provided with complete discretion regarding how

IRAS is implemented. But states have no ability to opt in or opt out of IRAS. PJM will issue

directives to curtail New Large Load customers without regard to the preference of individual

states. Failure to conform state policies to IRAS would risk subjecting all retail customers to

interruption when PJM issues curtailment directives—a consequence that is so severe as to leave

states with no option but to comply. IRAS effectively conscripts state authorities into enforcing a




                                                -2-
 federal policy respecting matters that have been left to the exclusive judgment and oversight of the

states under the FPA.

         The record in this proceeding demonstrates the risks of PJM’s top-down approach to retail

curtailment. As commenters point out, IRAS fails to account for the reliability contributions of

state peak-shaving programs and similar measures that have been implemented by the states to

encourage voluntary reductions by large load customers.6 Not only will this unduly discriminate

against New Large Loads that have invested in technologies to reduce their loads, but the

disconnect between IRAS and state programs has the potential to subject Electric Distributors to

conflicting regulatory obligations and uncertainty.7

         PJM accuses DCC of taking contradictory positions by arguing for “rejection of IRAS on

one hand in favor of state jurisdiction but then bemoans that if states take different positions on

curtailment, it will not be clear that IRAS will deliver its intended reliability benefits.”8 But the

real contradiction lies within PJM’s defense of IRAS. Because IRAS so clearly targets matters

within the exclusive authority of the states, PJM has no choice but to argue that the states retain

discretion over implementation of IRAS in an effort to justify its proposal. Yet, its repeated

assertions about state discretion, in turn, undercut PJM’s claims that IRAS can achieve its

objectives.

         While the jurisdictional defects in IRAS alone support rejection of PJM’s proposal, PJM

also has not demonstrated that IRAS is just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or



          6
            PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Comments of the Chief Energy Officer for the
Governor of Virginia at 2-5 (Sept. 3, 2026).
          7
            PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of the
New Jersey Board of Public Utilities at 4-5 (Sept. 18, 2026) (“[I]t is unclear whether EDCs will face penalties for not
curtailing the entire amount of the registered peak New Large Load amount directed by PJM, or if EDCs must curtail
other customers in order to meet this IRAS obligation.”).
          8
            PJM Answer at 28.


                                                        -3-
 preferential on its own terms. PJM does not offer any response to many of the objections that have

been expressed by DCC and other parties, and the responses that PJM does provide are largely

conclusory and do not respond to the substance of commenters’ concerns. For instance, DCC

demonstrated that the design of IRAS will result in customers in zones with New Large Loads

subsidizing rate reductions for other customers within the PJM footprint; yet, PJM’s Answer does

not acknowledge or address these concerns.9 PJM also does not offer any response to concerns

raised by DCC and others that IRAS will undermine the settled expectations of New Large Loads

that have made investment decisions.10

         PJM attempts to salvage IRAS by arguing that every aspect of its proposal is severable

and inviting the Commission to rewrite the proposal to cure its defects. PJM even goes so far as

to ask the Commission to impose a stand-alone requirement that all load-serving entities (“LSE”)

bring new capacity to serve New Large Loads. Other parties ask the Commission to strike aspects

of the IRAS framework that they argue go too far. But even with PJM’s consent, the Commission

has no authority under FPA Section 205 to “go beyond approval or rejection of a proposal to

adoption of an entirely different rate design.”11 And the Commission should decline PJM’s

invitation to do so here.

        Rather than approving a framework that conscripts state authorities into enforcing federal

curtailment policies, the Commission should reject the Filing and encourage PJM to work with

stakeholders and the states to develop emergency procedures that accommodate—rather than

dictate—the retail curtailment priorities of individual states. Alternatively, if the Commission



        9
           PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Motion to Intervene and Protest of the Data
Center Coalition at 22-23 (Sept. 3, 2026) (“DCC Protest”).
        10
           Id. at 30-34.
        11
            NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 115 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (internal quotations omitted)
(“NRG”).


                                                    -4-
 finds that PJM’s existing emergency procedures have been rendered unjust and unreasonable, it

should initiate an FPA Section 206 proceeding to develop reforms that respect the jurisdictional

boundaries established by the FPA. At a minimum, if the Commission does not reject IRAS

outright, it should direct PJM to establish a meaningful transition mechanism and delay

implementation until June 1, 2028 to provide New Large Loads and state authorities a reasonable

timeline to adapt.

       A.      PJM’s Justifications Cannot Cure The Jurisdictional Defects With IRAS

               1.       IRAS Is Premised On An Overly Broad View Of FERC’s Jurisdiction
                        That Cannot Be Squared With The FPA

       PJM argues that the jurisdictional concerns expressed by DCC and numerous other parties

in this proceeding are misplaced. According to PJM, whether IRAS “‘targets’ retail or wholesale

customers turns on the justification for the rule, not on whether or the extent to which the rule

affects or even compels action of retail or wholesale customers.”12 PJM then offers a series of

justifications that it claims eliminate any doubts about the legality of IRAS including that it will

“support[] system reliability in the PJM region” and provide a new tool to address situations where

supply shortfalls jeopardize system reliability.13

       It is worth pausing for a moment on the breadth of authority that PJM seeks to claim for

itself. Under PJM’s theory, the extent to which IRAS “affects or even compels action of retail”

customers is immaterial to the jurisdictional analysis.14 All that matters is whether PJM can

articulate some way in which its proposal will support reliability or allow it to more effectively

manage its system when supply is tight. But if the sole test for Commission jurisdiction is whether

a filing utility can articulate some nexus between the rule at issue and the reliability of the


       12
          PJM Answer at 19-20 (citing FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 265 (2016) (“EPSA”)).
       13
          Id. at 21.
       14
          Id. at 20 (emphasis added).


                                                   -5-
 transmission system, there is virtually no aspect of the production, delivery, or consumption of

electricity that would be beyond the reach of PJM and FERC. PJM could, on the same logic, adopt

tariff requirements that require utilities to construct new generation facilities to resolve supply

shortfalls, impose mandatory energy efficiency standards on their retail customers, or require all

retail customers to participate in a mandatory demand-response program of PJM’s design—each

time invoking the need to address supply shortfalls and manage transmission system reliability

when the system is stressed.

       But no precedent supports PJM’s theory of FERC’s jurisdiction.             And even if the

justifications offered by a filing utility were the sole benchmark for evaluating whether a proposal

was consistent with the jurisdictional boundaries established by the FPA, IRAS would not survive

scrutiny.

                  2.      PJM Misinterprets Applicable Precedent Defining The Respective
                          Responsibilities Of FERC And The States

       PJM’s arguments that the Commission need only consider PJM’s justification for IRAS

are based on an unduly narrow and selective reading of applicable court and Commission

precedent. While PJM relies heavily on FERC v. EPSA, nothing in that case stands for the

proposition that FERC may regulate any matter that has an impact on the reliability of wholesale

markets. To the contrary, the Court recognized that interpreting the FPA as providing FERC

authority to regulate any matter that affects wholesale markets would extend FERC’s power

beyond the scope of authority envisioned by Congress15 and that the FPA prohibited FERC from

approving rules that target matters within the exclusive authority of the states “no matter how




       15
            EPSA at 277-278.


                                               -6-
 direct, or dramatic, its impact on wholesale sales.”16 PJM’s interpretation of the scope of federal

authority cannot be squared with the Court’s reasoning.

        Nor did the Court confine itself to examining the justifications offered by the agency when

evaluating whether FERC’s actions exceeded the bounds established by Congress. Although the

Court noted the justifications offered by FERC in support of Order No. 745, the Court assigned

equal—if not more—weight to the fact that rules adopted by the Commission addressed only

“transactions occurring on the wholesale market.”17 “[W]hatever the effects at the retail level,

every aspect of the regulatory plan happens exclusively on the wholesale market and governs

exclusively that market’s rules.”18 As DCC explained in its Protest, this simply is not the case

with IRAS.19

        PJM argues that the Commission’s recent decision to approve Tri-State’s High Impact

Large Load Tariff (“HILT”) demonstrates that the FPA does not prevent transmission providers

from imposing obligations on utilities serving large loads merely because they “affect the quantity

or terms of retail rate regulation.”20 But PJM’s reliance on Tri-State overlooks the Commission’s

reason for approving the revised HILT proposal: it exclusively governed wholesale service to

utility members without seeking to dictate the rates, terms, and conditions of retail service.21 The

Commission was able to reach this conclusion with respect to Tri-State’s HILT proposal because

its terms and conditions were entirely limited to wholesale sales (e.g., evaluation fees, resource



         16
            Id. at 277-278 (“[I]f indirect or tangential impacts on wholesale electricity rates sufficed, FERC could
regulate now in one industry, now in another, changing a vast array of rules and practices to implement its vision of
reasonableness and justice. We cannot imagine that was what Congress had in mind.”).
         17
            Id. at 281.
         18
            Id.
         19
            DCC Protest at 8-15.
         20
            PJM Answer at 25-26 (quoting Tri-State Generation & Transmission Ass’n, Inc., 196 FERC ¶ 61,127
(2026) (“Tri-State”)).
         21
            Id. at PP 66-68.


                                                       -7-
 studies, deposit requirements, and associated agreements)22 and transmission service (e.g.,

transmission cost allocation rules, reliability and transmission planning criteria) to Tri-State’s

members.23 The Commission explained that Tri-State’s proposal thus did “not dictate the terms

or conditions of retail service” but merely established pro forma terms for taking transmission

service and provisions related to wholesale sales to its full requirements customers. 24 Nothing

about this arrangement, the Commission found, imposed requirements as to the retail arrangements

Tri-State’s members could enter into with their customers.25

       Unlike HILT, IRAS is not limited to the terms and conditions of wholesale sales or

transmission planning. To the contrary, IRAS seeks to prescribe resource procurement and

curtailment requirements for retail customers within the PJM region. PJM’s proposed tariff

revisions direct Electric Distributors to curtail “Eligible New Large Loads,” establish a default rate

for compensating customers for these curtailments to be recovered “in its retail rates,”26 and direct

Electric Distributors to recover the costs of these payments from other retail customers.

       PJM also argues that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit’s decision in New

Jersey Board of Public Utilities v. FERC affirming the Commission’s elimination of the state-

mandated exemption from the minimum offer price rule demonstrates that FERC has authority to

take steps to prevent the “state’s choices from adversely affecting wholesale capacity rates.”27 But

the rule at issue in NJ BPU is easily distinguishable from IRAS. NJ BPU concerned the rules

governing the submission of offers into the PJM capacity market. As in EPSA, the actions under



       22
          Id. at PP 12, 14.
       23
          Id. at PP 13, 16.
       24
          Id. at P 67.
       25
          Id. at P 66.
       26
          Filing, Proposed Tariff, Att. DD-4 § X(a).
       27
          PJM Answer at 27 (quoting N.J. Bd. of Pub. Util. v. FERC, 744 F.3d 74, 98 (3d Cir. 2014) (“NJ BPU”)).


                                                    -8-
 review in NJ BPU exclusively governed the rules for participating in the wholesale markets. IRAS,

in contrast, invades state authority over retail rates by seeking to exercise control over the

curtailment of retail customers and even the credits and charges passed through retail customers’

bills. Nothing in NJ BPU supports accepting IRAS.

        IRAS bears a striking resemblance to the “far-fetched example” the Court in EPSA offered

to illustrate the type of action that would unlawfully intrude on state authority—namely, a federally

imposed requirement “compelling every consumer to buy a certain amount of electricity on the

retail market.”28 IRAS effectively mandates that New Large Load customers procure sufficient

capacity to cover their demand consistent with PJM’s bring your own new capacity (“BYONC”)

requirements; if a customer does not, then PJM will issue instructions to Electric Distributors to

curtail service to customers to enforce PJM’s procurement mandate. Although the growth of large

loads has led PJM to propose frameworks that previously seemed far-fetched, the governing

jurisdictional principles remain the same: PJM and FERC cannot seek to regulate the rates, terms,

and conditions of retail service. And like the example provided by the Court in EPSA, IRAS

exceeds the authority granted to FERC under the FPA.

                 3.       PJM’s Statements And Tariff Language Support Rejection Of IRAS
                          As An Unlawful Intrusion On State Authority

        While PJM encourages the Commission to focus on the justifications offered by PJM,

PJM’s statements confirm that IRAS explicitly targets the rates, terms, and conditions of retail

service. Among other things, PJM’s statements make clear that IRAS establishes a policy that

retail customers must bring their own capacity or face service interruptions,29 seeks to identify and


        28
            EPSA at 280.
        29
            PJM Answer at 17 (“PJM intends to establish the policy that New Large Loads must bring new capacity
or PJM may request that they reduce their energy consumption to alleviate emergency conditions.”). See also id. at 3
(stating that absent compliance with PJM’s BYONC requirements, “New Large Loads must be flexible and, pursuant
to PJM’s operational needs, reduce their energy demands when called upon during system emergencies”).


                                                       -9-
 target retail customers that do not meet BYONC requirements for curtailment,30 establishes a

“default” rate and framework for Electric Distributors to pay retail customers that are curtailed

under IRAS,31 and directs Electric Distributors to recover these costs from other retail customers

through their retail rates.32 PJM also explains that IRAS is intended to ensure that states “re-

evaluate” their retail curtailment practices and “enlists” states to implement PJM’s proposed

framework.33

         The target of IRAS is readily apparent from PJM’s proposed tariff language as well.

Although PJM claims that IRAS does not dictate which customers will be curtailed, its tariff

language says otherwise. For instance, proposed Attachment DD-4 states that Electric Distributors

“shall execute . . . PJM’s directives to implement Interim Resource Adequacy Service Actions

among Eligible New Large Loads in the Electric Distributor’s zone/area.” 34 This language does

not provide Electric Distributors discretion regarding whether to curtail Eligible New Large Loads

within their zone. To the contrary, an Electric Distributor that curtailed retail customers other than

Eligible New Large Loads would be in direct violation of its obligations under the tariff.

         Likewise, PJM’s tariff language obligates Electric Distributors to implement a

compensation program that would provide Eligible New Large Loads with credits in their retail

             Filing, Transmittal Letter at 28 (stating that the Large Load Registry will be used to track Large Loads
within the PJM region to monitor whether they are complying with requirements to bring new capacity or should be
subject to IRAS).
          31
             Id. at 27 (explaining that Electric Distributors must “implement compensation program[s] consistent with”
PJM tariff); id. at 102 (“PJM is proposing a rate for IRAS that is equal to 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate”);
id. (“[A] rate of zero dollars for IRAS would apply where Eligible New Large Loads waive in their retail rates receipt
of compensation for the provision of wholesale Interim Resource Adequacy Service”); id. at 104 (“[T]he IRAS rate is
intended to be conjoined with retail rates and ultimately paid to Eligible New Large Loads that reflects a discount on
capacity costs commensurate with the impact of Interim Resource Adequacy Service on addressing resource adequacy
issues.”).
          32
             Id. at 104 (explaining that payments to retail customers curtailed under IRAS will be recovered from retail
loads consistent with Electric Distributors’ state-approved programs).
          33
             Id. at 3, 107. See also PJM Answer at 3 (stating that IRAS establishes a “region-wide response” to “guide
and provide a framework for the PJM states’ various disparate approaches”).
          34
             Filing, Proposed Tariff, Att. DD-4 § III(a).


                                                        - 10 -
 rates equal to 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate.35 Notably, while PJM characterizes its

default rate as a cap that can be modified by state regulators, the only exception from this

requirement recognized in the tariff is if the Eligible New Large Load agrees to “accept in its retail

rates” a sum lower than the default rate or “waive[s] receipt in its retail rates” of the default rate.36

And if state regulators do not take action to permit implementation of these requirements, PJM

states that Eligible New Large Loads may initiate state regulatory proceedings to enforce their

rights to receive compensation.37

        PJM’s arguments that states will retain full discretion regarding how IRAS is implemented

cannot save IRAS. IRAS exhibits none of the “solicitude towards the States” that the Court relied

upon in upholding the program at issue in EPSA.38 As discussed above, the level of discretion that

PJM claims IRAS affords to the states is simply not reflected in the tariff. Nor do states have the

ability to “opt in” or “opt out” of IRAS. If IRAS is approved, PJM will instruct Electric

Distributors to curtail New Large Loads that have not complied with BYONC requirements

regardless of the preferences of state authorities. And state authorities will have little choice but

to modify their policies to align with IRAS to avoid the risk that the brunt of PJM’s curtailments

will be borne by retail customers generally rather than the Eligible New Large Loads targeted by

PJM.

        Ultimately, PJM’s arguments about the discretion of state regulators miss the point. If the

decisions at issue—how retail customers are served, which retail customers are subject to

curtailment, under what terms, and at what rates—are properly within the states’ exclusive



        35
            Id., Att. DD-4 § X(a).
        36
            Id., Att. DD-4 § X(c)(ii).
         37
            Id., Transmittal Letter at 106-107 (“[I]f states decline to act, Eligible New Large Loads could initiate
regulatory proceedings to develop retail pathways to recover wholesale IRAS rates.”).
         38
            EPSA at 287.


                                                      - 11 -
 authority, then it is not PJM’s place to design the program that frames and compels those decisions

in the first instance. Delegating implementation to the states does not change the fact that PJM is

seeking to establish procurement requirements for large load customers, define the conditions

under which curtailment is triggered, and prescribe a default compensation rate that is intended to

be embedded in retail rate structures. These are retail policy and ratemaking choices and no

amount of state-level implementation discretion transforms them into wholesale ones.39

         B.       PJM Has Not Demonstrated That Curtailing Eligible New Large Loads Before
                  Requiring Demand Resources To Perform Is Just, Reasonable, And
                  Consistent With Cost Causation Requirements

         Under IRAS, Eligible New Large Loads will be required to bear the costs of Demand

Resources cleared through PJM’s forward capacity market, but will not enjoy the benefits of this

capacity. While Demand Resources are committed through the capacity market to “avoid periods

of involuntar[y] firm load shed or blackouts,”40 PJM now proposes to curtail service to Network

Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) customers serving Eligible New Large Loads prior to

asking Demand Resources to fulfill their capacity commitments. Yet, PJM continues to maintain

that it is just and reasonable to force Eligible New Large Loads to bear the costs of these capacity

commitments.

         PJM does not deny that IRAS will result in Eligible New Large Loads paying for Demand

Resources that will not be used to provide them with service. Instead, PJM claims that this

treatment is justified because Eligible New Large Loads “failed to cover their capacity

the same result.”) (internal quotation and citations omitted).
          40
             PJM, Powering Reliability Through Market Design: Addressing Rising Demand and Constrained Supply,
and Stimulating Investment To Support Durable Reliability at 14 (May 6, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-through-market-
design.pdf.


                                                         - 12 -
 obligations.”41 But that is a non-answer to the concerns expressed by DCC and other commenters

that PJM’s proposal will force customers “to pay for capacity without receiving commensurate

reliability benefits.”42 Even if a New Large Load has not procured capacity that complies with

PJM’s BYONC requirements, that does not change the fact that these loads will pay the cost of

capacity procured through the PJM markets. And PJM has not demonstrated that it is just and

reasonable to require Eligible New Large Loads to bear the cost of Demand Resources when these

customers will be curtailed prior to when the Demand Resources they pay for have been deployed.

       PJM also claims that calling on Demand Resources prior to curtailing Eligible New Large

Loads would be inappropriate because it would reduce the incentive for such loads to meet

BYONC requirements.43 But the fact that a proposed rate may incentivize a particular customer

class to take certain actions does not inherently render the rate as a whole just and reasonable.

Indeed, by PJM’s logic, it would also be appropriate to curtail Eligible New Large Loads before

PJM takes any other action to maintain reliability or to prevent Eligible New Large Loads from

receiving service entirely since taking these actions would incentivize Eligible New Large Loads

to meet BYONC requirements.

       PJM further argues that its proposal to curtail Eligible New Large Loads before deploying

Demand Resources is justified since it is consistent with its current approach to curtailing non-

firm transmission service after economic generation and before Pre-Emergency Load Management

because both non-firm transmission customers and Eligible New Large Loads have transacted in

the PJM energy markets without having secured any capacity.44 But PJM’s comparison of Eligible




       41
          PJM Answer at 33-34.
       42
          DCC Protest at 17.
       43
          PJM Answer at 34.
       44
          Id.


                                             - 13 -
 New Large Loads to non-firm transmission customers overlooks that Eligible New Large Loads

in fact pay for capacity while non-firm transmission customers do not. As PJM’s Answer

concedes, “[t]hose entities that fail to arrange for BYONC will still be paying for capacity…”45

PJM’s entire basis for comparing the curtailment of non-firm transmission customers to Eligible

New Large Loads is thus unfounded.

        PJM attempts to justify its approach by noting that customers that are curtailed under IRAS

will be eligible to receive compensation equal to 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate. PJM

overlooks, however, that Eligible New Large Loads will be eligible for compensation only during

the limited intervals each year when they are subject to curtailment under IRAS while they will be

required to pay capacity charges reflecting the cost of Demand Resources every day during the

Delivery Year even though these resources are not available to meet their load.46 PJM has not

provided any evidence demonstrating that providing a limited reimbursement in a subset of hours

will offset the costs borne by Eligible New Large Loads for capacity that they do not benefit from

or otherwise result in these customers bearing costs that are roughly commensurate with the

benefits they receive. PJM’s claim that the availability of compensation addresses any concerns

rings particularly hollow given PJM’s repeated statements that this compensation may be reduced

to zero.47

        PJM also attempts to justify its proposal by introducing the concept of “Demand Resource

fatigue.”48 PJM explains that the more often that Demand Resources are called upon, the more




        45
            Id. at 53.
        46
            Id. at 55-56.
         47
            Id. at 55 (acknowledging that “the IRAS compensation rate may be reduced, even to 0%, by the states
and/or appropriate RERRAs at the retail level.”).
         48

                                                    - 14 -
 likely it is that Demand Resources will become unwilling to provide Demand Response. 49 As a

result, PJM indicates that although “Demand Resources are paid the same daily rate as other

Capacity Resources,” it cannot call upon Demand Resources to perform in the same way it does

other Capacity Resources.50 PJM thus contends that it is appropriate not to call upon Demand

Resources until after it has curtailed retail loads.

        PJM’s concession that it is paying Demand Resources as Capacity Resources yet cannot

expect such resources to perform as Capacity Resources and thus will instead curtail retail loads

is alarming. “All supply-side capacity resources, including Demand Resources, are required to

meet the Capacity Performance requirements.”51 Demand Resources have been paid over $1.5

billion over the past two Base Residual Auctions alone on the basis that they can meet these

requirements and maintain the reliability of the PJM system for the benefit of load.52 If PJM

believes that it cannot rely on Demand Resources to consistently perform when called upon for

the benefit of load that pays for their performance, it should take actions to reform its tariff to

reflect that it cannot rely on these resources in the same way it does other Capacity Resources. But

PJM should not be permitted to excuse Demand Resources from providing the capacity that

customers have paid them for and instead curtail retail customers.53
